power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Alternative polyadenylation contributes extensively to transcript diversification and is particularly prominent during neuronal diKerentiation.

CSTF2 encodes an RNA-binding subunit of the cleavage stimulation factor complex and has previously been associated with X-linked intellectual disability through a single Asp50Ala missense variant with increased RNA-binding activity.

Here, we identify seven rare CSTF2 variants in ten hemizygous male probands with intellectual disability, global developmental delay and/or autism spectrum disorder, including missense, nonsense, splice-site, and frameshift variants.
We functionally assessed selected variants by ectopic expression in CSTF2-depleted HEK293T cells, followed by total and 3′-end-proximal RNA sequencing.
Phe19Leu, Gln543Ter and Leu555Ser markedly impaired CSTF2 function.

These variants predominantly reduced the usage of strong, evolutionarily conserved intronic polyadenylation sites with prominent GU-rich sequences, while increasing the usage of downstream sites within terminal 3′UTRs.
In contrast, the previously reported Asp50Ala variant produced an opposing pattern, with preferential activation of intronic polyadenylation sites, consistent with its increased RNA-binding activity.
These findings data provide genetic and functional support for CSTF2 as an X-linked intellectual.

text.text: Thus, inactivating CSTF2 variants dysregulate polyadenylation by predominantly suppressing a strong evolutionary conserved set of intronic sites.
Here we identified loss-of-function variants in polyadenylation factor CSTF2 in hemizygous probands with intellectual disability, global developmental delay and autism spectrum disorder.
For a subset of missense variants, we showed that they dysregulate polyadenylation by impairing functions of evolutionary conserved functional domains of CSTF2.

This functional evidence implicating CSTF2 in RNA cleavage and polyadenylation provides a plausible molecular mechanism for the neurodevelopmental phenotypes observed in the cohort, particularly speech and language delay, intellectual disability and autistic features.
Notably, the previously reported familial Asp50Ala variant was associated with mild intellectual disability and speech diKiculties, without motor delay or reported autistic features 22 .

text.text: Its distinct functional eKects contrast with those observed for variants in our cohort, many of which arose de novo, despite the X-linked inheritance of CSTF2.
These findings suggest that variant-specific eKects on polyadenylation may influence the severity and spectrum of neurodevelopmental manifestations.
Our RNA-seq analysis showed strongest dysregulation of polyadenylation by Phe19Leu and Gln543ter and Leu555Ser variants.

While Met179Arg and Gly40Arg showed no significant and very mild eKect on polyadenylation, respectively, caution should be applied in their classification as overexpression assays can naturally mask the eKects of destabilising variants.

In line with this, both these variants are predicted to be destabilising by the FoldX algorithm (Met179Arg ΔΔG = 2.96 and Gly40Arg ΔΔG = 3.34) requiring further experiments to understand their potential pathogenicity.

Importantly, the individual with the Met179Arg variant, with autism spectrum disorder and mild intellectual disability, also carried a 16p11.2 deletion (arr[hg19]16p11.2(29656684_30190568)x1), consistent with a recurrent proximal (BP4-BP5) deletion in individuals with variably penetrant neurodevelopmental phenotypes, including intellectual disability, speech delay, learning diKiculties, motor coordination abnormalities and . behavioural phenotypes [36] [37] [38] .
text.formatted: Importantly, the individual with the Met179Arg variant, with autism spectrum disorder and mild intellectual disability, also carried a 16p11.2 deletion (arr[hg19]16p11.2(29656684_30190568)x1), consistent with a recurrent proximal (BP4-BP5) deletion in individuals with variably penetrant neurodevelopmental phenotypes, including intellectual disability, speech delay, learning diKiculties, motor coordination abnormalities and . behavioural phenotypes <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref> .

text.text: While we cannot exclude that the CSTF2 variant may be contributing to his features, these may be attributable to the 16p11.2 microdeletion.

Overexpression of Phe19Leu and Gln543ter and Leu555Ser variants suppresses activity of hundreds of intronic polyadenylation sites and activates hundreds of polyadenylation sites downstream in 3'UTRs of corresponding genes.

Based on significantly higher GU-content downstream of suppressed sites we propose that inactivation of CSTF2 directly suppresses intronic sites (and a small fraction of suppressed sites in 3'UTR) while downstream activation is likely a secondary eKect.
This is also supported by higher predicted strength of the suppressed sites.

Previous reports demonstrated the role of CSTF2 in activation of intronic polyadenylation in immune related genes 16, 39 ; our results highlight CSTF2 as a global regulator of intronic polyadenylation.

text.text: Importantly, we detected a strong suppressive eKect on a CSTF3 intronic site known to function as a sensor in an evolutionary conserved feedback autoregulatory loop controlling the state of polyadenylation in cells 31 .
text.formatted: Importantly, we detected a strong suppressive eKect on a CSTF3 intronic site known to function as a sensor in an evolutionary conserved feedback autoregulatory loop controlling the state of polyadenylation in cells <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> .

text.text: Strikingly, the observed suppressive eKect of these variants on polyadenylation was stronger and opposite from the moderate activating eKect of overexpression of the Asp50Ala variant.

While the degree of dysregulation by investigated variants is likely dependent on the state of polyadenylation in a cell (overall expression and activity of polyadenylation factors), the directionality of dysregulation is expected to be constant.
Therefore, our data strongly suggest "gain-of-function" eKect of Asp50Ala in line with previously published in vitro experimental data 22.
text.formatted: Therefore, our data strongly suggest "gain-of-function" eKect of Asp50Ala in line with previously published in vitro experimental data <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref>.

text.text: More importantly these data suggest that CSTF2 activity and/or expression tightly regulates polyadenylation in a balanced manner with both activating and inactivating variants inducing intellectual disability.

Nevertheless, we would expect loss-of-function variants to occur more frequently than gain-of-function variants, as random genetic variation is more likely to disrupt existing protein function than to confer enhanced or novel activity 40, 41.
text.formatted: Nevertheless, we would expect loss-of-function variants to occur more frequently than gain-of-function variants, as random genetic variation is more likely to disrupt existing protein function than to confer enhanced or novel activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">40,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref>.

text.text: Taken together our data suggest that CSTF2 Phe19Leu and Gln543ter and Leu555Ser variants are likely inactivating "loss-of-function" variants.
Together with additional ACMG/AMP criteria 42 , we suggest these variants can be classified as "Likely Pathogenic" [PS3, PM2, PP3, PP2, PM6 (in 2 of 3)].
text.formatted: Together with additional ACMG/AMP criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42</ref> , we suggest these variants can be classified as "Likely Pathogenic" [PS3, PM2, PP3, PP2, PM6 (in 2 of 3)].

text.text: Overall, our data strengthens the association between CSTF2 and intellectual disability, paving the way for increasing the diagnostic yield.

Recessive loss-of-function variants in the core polyadenylation factors CLP1 and CPSF3 cause severe neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by global developmental delay, . microcephaly, and brain malformations 43, 44 .
text.formatted: Recessive loss-of-function variants in the core polyadenylation factors CLP1 and CPSF3 cause severe neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by global developmental delay, . microcephaly, and brain malformations <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44</ref> .

text.text: Our data suggest that CSTF2 deficiency results in a considerably milder phenotype.

This potentially reflects the distinct specificity of these proteins: in our model CSTF2 regulates polyadenylation at a subset of sites with prominent GU-rich downstream tracts, whereas CLP1 and CPSF3 are likely more broadly required for cleavage and polyadenylation of most pre-mRNAs.

Consequently, CSTF2 loss is expected to have more transcript-specific eKects rather than causing a global defect in mRNA 3′-end processing (with a similar intronic to 3'UTR polyadenylation shift observed after overexpression of a pathogenic CLP1 variant in a neuronal model 45 ).
text.formatted: Consequently, CSTF2 loss is expected to have more transcript-specific eKects rather than causing a global defect in mRNA 3′-end processing (with a similar intronic to 3'UTR polyadenylation shift observed after overexpression of a pathogenic CLP1 variant in a neuronal model <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45</ref> ).

text.text: The milder phenotype may also be explained by partial functional compensation from its paralogue, CSTF2t 46 .
text.formatted: The milder phenotype may also be explained by partial functional compensation from its paralogue, CSTF2t <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46</ref> .

text.text: Further studies in disease-relevant models are needed to determine how defects in polyadenylation drive distinct neurodevelopmental disorders, and why disruption of diKerent components of the polyadenylation machinery results in variable clinical severity.
Taken together, our work provides the first comprehensive characterisation of inactivating CSTF2 variants, and establishes CSTF2 as a conclusive X-linked intellectual disability gene.

Our findings significantly expand the spectrum of polyadenylation disrupting disorders underlying intellectual disability, highlight the role of CSTF2 in regulation of intronic polyadenylation and suggest an important role in human neurodevelopment.
